m: Something that deviates from what is expected.
t: Same as « anomalie »: the point off the even line.
Feeling against: the opposite of sympathy. « Antipathie ».

m: To pacify by giving in to demands.
t: Appease = « apaiser »: bringing peace. Munich 1938 = appeasement.
Same as « ardu »: a steep climb.

m: With suspicion or disapproval (to look askance).
e: Origin uncertain, 1500s; perhaps from Italian a scancio (sideways).
t: Looking at someone sideways: « regarder de travers ».

m: The quality of being trite or unoriginal.
e: French banalité, from banal, from the feudal ban (Frankish): the lord’s oven used by all.
t: Same as « banalité ». The village four banal again.

e: Old English bolster (a long pillow). Germanic. To prop up with a cushion.
t: A bolster is a long pillow propping you up. Data that bolsters your case.

e: French capricieux, from Italian capriccio (a sudden start, whim), perhaps from capra (goat) for its leaps.
t: A goat leaping unpredictably: « capricieux ».

e: Latin contritio (grinding), from conterere (to grind, crush). A heart crushed by guilt.
t: Same as « contrition » in confession: a heart ground down by guilt.

e: Middle English cravant (defeated), probably from Old French cravanté (crushed).
t: Defeated and crushed: a craven surrender.
Same as « délétère »: « une ambiance délétère ».
« Des manœuvres dilatoires »: stalling tactics.

m: Not influenced by strong emotion; impartial.
t: Without passion: a dispassionate analysis.
Sowing seeds everywhere: « disséminer ».

m: Threats or pressure used to force someone.
t: From dur: signed under duress = sous la contrainte.

m: Using no more than necessary; thrifty (also: economical with the truth).
t: House management. On the GRE: economical prose = no wasted words.

e: Latin aedificare (to build): aedes (building) + facere. Building up the soul.
t: Same as « édifiant »: building (édifice) your character.
Efficacious = « efficace ». Used of remedies.

m: To draw out a response or fact.
t: Lure out a reaction. Not illicit (illegal).

e: Latin eruditus, from erudire (to instruct): e- + rudis (rough). Taking the roughness out.
t: Same as « érudit »: no longer rude/rough.

m: Understood by only a small group.
e: Greek esōterikos (inner), from esō (within). Teachings for inner disciples only.
t: Same as « ésotérique »: for the inner circle.

m: Very attentive to detail; hard to please.
t: Careful: « fastidieux » = tedious. Fastidious = maniaque, fussy.
Heraclitus: everything flows. A market in flux.

m: Secretive; trying not to be noticed.
t: Same as « furtif »: moving like a thief.

e: Old English hergian (to ravage, raid), related to here (army). Germanic.
t: Raided by an army of emails. A harried consultant on a Sunday.

e: Latin ignominia: in- (not) + nomen (name). Loss of one’s good name.
t: Same as « ignominieux »: losing your name.

e: in- + partial, from Latin pars (part). Not taking a part.
t: Same as « impartial ».

m: Not showing care for the consequences.
t: Same as « imprudent »: not foreseeing.
Breaking « le décorum ».

e: Latin Iovialis (of Jupiter). Astrologers held those born under Jupiter to be happy.
t: Same as « jovial »: born under jolly Jupiter (Jove).
Straight from French « maladroit ».

e: From Samuel Maverick (1803–1870), a Texas rancher who refused to brand his cattle; unbranded calves were called mavericks.
t: The unbranded calf wandering free from the herd. Also Top Gun’s pilot.
Mendacity sounds like « mensonge », and that’s exactly what it is: a habit of lying.
Building the wrong meaning. Contrast with construe.
Careful: « mondain » = society/high life. Mundane = ordinary everyday stuff.

m: So surprised one doesn’t know how to react.
e: Latin non plus (no more): a state where nothing more can be said.
t: « Non plus »: you have nothing more to say. Means baffled, not calm.

m: A subtle difference in meaning or expression.
t: Straight from French: shades like those of a cloud (nue).
Same as « opulence ». Versailles’ Hall of Mirrors.
Same as « péjoratif »: making it sound worse.

m: To calm or soothe someone angry.
t: Placare: same root as implacable and plaire. Placate an angry client.

m: A strong verbal or written attack.
t: Same as « polémique »: war (polemos) by words.

m: To put forward as fact or a basis for argument.
t: To posit = « poser » a hypothesis on the table.

e: Anglo-French rebuker (to beat back), from Old French bukier (to strike).
t: Beat back verbally: a sharp rebuke from the partner.

e: Old French reprochier, from Vulgar Latin repropiare (to bring back near).
t: Same as « reprocher ». Beyond reproach = irréprochable.
Same as « spécieux »: pretty on the surface, false inside.
Pulled tight (stringere, as in stricte). Stringent regulations.
Solus = alone: the sulky teen alone in his room.
Same as « timoré ». Timor = fear.
Passing through: « transitoire ».
Same as « tronquer »: cut down to the trunk.
